blocks.text: A 30-year-old builder notices a lump that appears in his groin when he lifts and disappears when he lies down. In another bed, a man with a long history of liver disease vomits bright blood from veins at the lower end of the oesophagus. In both cases the diagnosis comes from knowing where vessels and openings lie.

blocks.markdown: The **inguinal ligament** runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the **pubic tubercle**. Groin hernias are classified by where they emerge relative to this ligament and the pubic tubercle, and by their relation to the **inferior epigastric vessels**, which arise from the external iliac vessels and ascend on the deep surface of the rectus abdominis.

blocks.title: Hernia
blocks.text: The protrusion of a viscus or part of one through an opening in the wall that normally contains it. It has a sac, a neck and contents. Strangulation occurs when the blood supply of the contents is compromised.

rows: Not related directly; passes through the femoral canal
Persistent processus vaginalis; may enter scrotum
Acquired weakness of the posterior wall
High, because of the narrow neck
blocks.caption: Distinguishing the three groin hernias.

blocks.title: Classifying a hernia
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old man has a groin lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle that descends into the scrotum. At operation the neck lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Which hernia is it and why?

steps.text: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle points to an inguinal hernia, not a femoral hernia.
A neck lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels means it passes through the deep inguinal ring.
Descent into the scrotum along the spermatic cord fits the course of the processus vaginalis.
This is an indirect inguinal hernia.

blocks.markdown: The **femoral canal** is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath. Its borders are the inguinal ligament in front, the pectineal ligament behind, the lacunar ligament medially and the femoral vein laterally. It normally contains fat and a lymph node. A femoral hernia enters the canal, has a narrow, rigid neck formed by these ligaments and is therefore prone to strangulation; it presents below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

**Arterial supply of the lower limb.** The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament. The femoral artery gives off the **profunda femoris** (deep femoral) artery and continues as the superficial femoral artery through the adductor canal to the popliteal artery. The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery (which becomes the dorsalis pedis) and the posterior tibial artery (and the peroneal artery). Pulses can be felt at the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries.

Limb perfusion is assessed using the **ankle-brachial index (ABI)**, the ratio of the systolic blood pressure at the ankle to the systolic pressure in the arm. Values around 1.0 are normal, and an ABI below about 0.9 suggests significant arterial disease; ranges vary slightly by guideline.

blocks.caption: Ankle-brachial index; pressures are systolic pressures in mmHg.

blocks.title: Calculating an ABI
blocks.prompt: A man with calf pain on walking has a systolic pressure of 150 mmHg in the arm and 105 mmHg at the posterior tibial artery. Calculate the ABI.

steps.text: Identify the ankle pressure, 105 mmHg, and the brachial pressure, 150 mmHg.
Compare with 0.9: the value of 0.70 is well below it, indicating significant arterial narrowing.

blocks.markdown: **Collateral circulation.** When a main artery is blocked, blood reaches the distal limb through anastomoses. Around the hip, the cruciate and trochanteric anastomoses link branches of the profunda femoris with gluteal and circumflex arteries. Around the knee, the **genicular anastomosis** links the genicular branches of the popliteal artery with descending branches of the femoral and branches of the tibial arteries. Occlusion of the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal can be partly bypassed through the profunda femoris and genicular anastomoses, which is why symptoms may appear only during exercise.

**Portosystemic anastomoses.** The portal system drains the gut to the liver. At certain sites portal tributaries communicate with systemic veins. If portal pressure rises, blood is shunted into these channels, which dilate as **varices**.

blocks.title: Direct or indirect: the epigastric vessels decide
blocks.text: Indirect hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring; direct hernias bulge medial to them. Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

points: Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle (indirect lateral, direct medial to the inferior epigastric vessels); femoral hernias lie below and lateral and strangulate easily.

The femoral artery gives the profunda femoris and continues to the popliteal artery; collaterals include the genicular anastomosis, and ABI (ankle systolic over brachial systolic) screens for ischaemia.
Portosystemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anorectal junction and umbilicus produce varices when portal pressure is raised.

questions.stem: A groin lump lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle in an elderly woman. Which hernia is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is characteristic of a femoral hernia.
distractorRationale.b: Direct hernias lie above and medial to the tubercle.
distractorRationale.c: Indirect hernias also lie above and medial to the tubercle.
distractorRationale.d: Obturator hernias do not usually present as a groin lump in this position.

questions.explanation: A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament into the femoral canal, so it lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is more common in women.

questions.stem: Why is a femoral hernia more likely to strangulate than a direct inguinal hernia?

options.text: Its neck is narrow and bounded by rigid ligaments
It passes through the deep inguinal ring

questions.correctOptionText: Its neck is narrow and bounded by rigid ligaments

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the narrow neck bordered by the lacunar and inguinal ligaments traps contents.
distractorRationale.b: Femoral hernias do have a sac.
distractorRationale.c: Passing through the deep ring describes an indirect hernia.
distractorRationale.d: The femoral artery lies lateral to the canal and is not its content.

questions.explanation: The femoral canal is small and bounded by ligaments on three sides and the vein laterally, so a hernia through it has a narrow neck.

questions.stem: At operation, a hernia sac is found medial to the inferior epigastric vessels and does not pass through the deep inguinal ring. Which type is it?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: direct hernias are medial to the vessels.
distractorRationale.b: Indirect hernias pass lateral to the vessels.
distractorRationale.c: Femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament.
distractorRationale.d: Spigelian hernias occur at the linea semilunaris.

questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric vessels are the divider: indirect lateral, direct medial. Direct hernias push through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

questions.stem: A woman with leg pain on walking has a brachial systolic pressure of 140 mmHg and an ankle systolic pressure of 84 mmHg. Calculate her ankle-brachial index (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: ABI = 84 divided by 140 = 0.60. This is well below 0.9, indicating significant arterial narrowing in the limb.

questions.stem: A patient has blockage of the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal but has a warm foot at rest. Which collateral route is most important?

options.text: Profunda femoris branches linking to the genicular anastomosis
Inferior epigastric artery to the popliteal artery

questions.correctOptionText: Profunda femoris branches linking to the genicular anastomosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: profunda femoris perforators and branches reach the genicular anastomosis around the knee.
distractorRationale.b: The great saphenous vein is a vein.
distractorRationale.c: The obturator artery supplies the thigh adductors, not the foot.
distractorRationale.d: The inferior epigastric artery supplies the abdominal wall.

questions.explanation: Blood bypasses the block through the profunda femoris and its branches that join the genicular anastomosis. This explains why limb survival is possible despite occlusion.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis has dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus. Which anastomosis is responsible?

options.text: Paraumbilical veins linking to the superficial epigastric veins
Superior rectal to middle rectal veins

questions.correctOptionText: Paraumbilical veins linking to the superficial epigastric veins

distractorRationale.a: Correct: paraumbilical veins open up to produce caput medusae.
distractorRationale.d: This causes retroperitoneal varices, not visible periumbilical veins.

questions.explanation: When portal pressure is high, blood flows via paraumbilical veins into the superficial epigastric veins on the abdominal wall. The visible dilated veins are called caput medusae.

questions.stem: Portal hypertension causes oesophageal varices because the left gastric vein, a portal tributary, communicates with veins draining to which system?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oesophageal veins drain to the azygos system.
distractorRationale.b: The hepatic veins carry blood from the liver.
distractorRationale.c: The inferior mesenteric vein is a portal tributary.
distractorRationale.d: The great saphenous vein is in the leg.

questions.explanation: Portal blood diverts through the gastro-oesophageal anastomosis into oesophageal veins that drain to the azygos system. These thin-walled veins dilate and may bleed.

questions.stem: Explain how the anatomy distinguishes a femoral hernia from an inguinal hernia, and why a femoral hernia is dangerous.
markingGuide: Femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
Femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament.
Neck is narrow and bounded by rigid ligaments.
questions.explanation: The relation to the inguinal ligament and pubic tubercle separates the two. The tight femoral canal makes the neck narrow and the contents prone to ischaemia.

questions.stem: Describe the arterial supply of the lower limb from the external iliac artery to the foot and explain how collateral circulation helps in chronic occlusion.
markingGuide: External iliac to femoral artery at inguinal ligament.
Profunda femoris branch; superficial femoral continues.
Popliteal artery then anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
Collaterals: profunda femoris and genicular anastomosis.
Anastomoses maintain flow around a chronic block.
questions.explanation: The main trunk is accompanied by branches that join one another around joints. When a segment narrows slowly, these channels enlarge and keep the foot perfused.

questions.stem: Explain why portal hypertension leads to oesophageal varices, haemorrhoids and caput medusae.
markingGuide: Portal and systemic veins communicate at specific sites.
Raised portal pressure reverses flow into the systemic side.
Oesophagus: left gastric and oesophageal veins.
Rectum: superior rectal and middle/inferior rectal veins.
questions.explanation: These anastomoses are normally small and carry low flow, but when pressure in the portal system rises they dilate to bypass the liver.
